overview: Eversource Energy is a Springfield, Massachusetts-headquartered public utility holding company (formerly Northeast Utilities) that delivers electricity and natural gas to approximately 4.5 million customers across Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire through regulated subsidiaries CL&P, NSTAR Electric, PSNH/Eversource NH, NSTAR Gas, Eversource Gas of Massachusetts (EGMA) and Yankee Gas. It exited both its water utility business (Aquarion Water, sold June 30, 2026) and its offshore wind generation interests (South Fork, Revolution Wind, Sunrise Wind, divested 2023-2024) to become a pure-play, wires-and-pipes regulated T&D utility. Earnings are driven almost entirely by rate-regulated electric and gas distribution and electric transmission investment rather than competitive generation.

business_model.summary: Eversource earns regulated returns on invested capital (rate base) in electric distribution, electric transmission and natural gas distribution across three New England states, plus FERC-regulated transmission formula-rate returns. Growth comes from a large, multi-year capital investment program (grid modernization, resiliency, electrification-related infrastructure) that grows rate base, with earnings realized through base rate cases, performance-based rate (PBR) mechanisms, and annual transmission formula-rate true-ups rather than sales volume growth.
business_model.customer_type: Regulated residential, commercial and industrial retail customers (B2C/B2B) plus wholesale transmission customers (other utilities/ISO-NE); revenue and allowed returns set by state PUCs (PURA in CT, DPU in MA, PUC in NH) and FERC
business_model.geographic_mix: Connecticut (CL&P, Yankee Gas), Massachusetts (NSTAR Electric, NSTAR Gas, EGMA), New Hampshire (PSNH/Eversource NH) - all within New England; no material international or unregulated generation exposure

main_competitors: Avangrid/National Grid USA (New England neighbors, not direct market competitors)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest electric and gas utility holding company in New England, operating as a franchised monopoly in each of its service territories; not in direct market competition for retail customers but competes industry-wide for regulatory capital allocation, equity investor capital, and favorable rate-case/legislative outcomes versus peer utilities

moat_factors.description: Exclusive right to serve electric/gas customers in its territories under state franchise law; no competitor can build parallel wires or pipes
Largest New England utility with a growing ~$26.5B five-year capital plan supporting an above-average 8%+ rate base CAGR
T&D infrastructure requires enormous upfront capital and decades-long permitting, deterring new entrants

moat_factors.factor: Diversification across three state jurisdictions and FERC transmission
moat_factors.description: Spreads regulatory risk, though Connecticut has recently been the most adversarial jurisdiction

weaknesses: Heavy, recurring reliance on constructive regulatory outcomes in three separate jurisdictions plus FERC; limited ability to pass through disallowed costs
Connecticut regulator (PURA) has a track record of storm-cost disallowances, ROE reductions and public criticism of the company, creating earned-vs-allowed ROE gaps
High leverage/elevated debt load (D/E ~1.8x, net debt/EBITDA ~5.7x per screen data) constrains financial flexibility and credit-rating cushion
Residual, hard-to-size offshore wind cost-sharing exposure (Revolution Wind) despite having fully exited ownership
No longer has water utility diversification after the Aquarion sale, slightly narrowing the regulated asset base

growth_drivers: $26.5 billion five-year (2026-2030) capital investment plan, up from $24.2B (2025-29) and $23.1B (2024-28), concentrated in electric distribution (grid modernization, resiliency, reliability) and electric transmission - not generation - driving ~8%+ rate base growth
FERC-regulated transmission investment (including an ISO-NE-selected Eversource/Avangrid project worth an incremental ~$700 million) offers a steadier, less state-regulatory-dependent growth avenue
Performance-based rate (PBR) mechanisms in Massachusetts and New Hampshire provide more predictable, formulaic rate increases versus traditional CT rate litigation
Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) rollout in Massachusetts (500,000+ meters installed) supporting grid modernization and potential future efficiency/demand-response revenue

Simplified, de-risked business mix post-divestitures (Aquarion water sale closed June 30, 2026 for ~$2.4B enterprise value/~$1.7B net equity proceeds used for debt paydown; full exit from offshore wind ownership) lets management and capital markets focus purely on the regulated wires-and-pipes growth story
Reaffirmed long-term 5-7% cumulative non-GAAP EPS growth through 2030, with management guiding toward the upper half of that range by 2028
Electrification trends (EVs, heat pumps, data center/large load interconnection demand) in New England providing a secular tailwind for incremental grid investment

business.description: PURA has repeatedly disallowed storm costs (~$500M disallowed in 2026 decision including ~$397M of retroactive carrying charges), cut allowed ROEs (e.g., Yankee Gas reduced to 9.32% from a 9.48% base), and faced public criticism from the Attorney General; a pending CT base rate case outcome remains a swing factor

business.risk: Execution risk on an expanding, multi-billion-dollar capital plan
business.description: Capital plan has grown every year (from $23.1B to $26.5B); cost overruns, supply chain/tariff inflation, or construction delays could compress realized ROE versus plan

Despite exiting ownership of South Fork, Revolution Wind and Sunrise Wind, Eversource retains cost-sharing obligations on Revolution Wind (up to $240M of shared capex overruns plus other make-whole provisions); two 2025 federal stop-work orders drove a cumulative ~$164M-plus of incremental charges in 2025-2026, with analyst estimates of worst-case exposure exceeding $700M in an abandonment scenario
The company is now a pure electric/gas T&D utility with no water segment buffering regulatory risk concentration

financial.description: Debt/equity ~1.8x and net debt/EBITDA ~5.7x (per latest screen data); S&P downgraded Eversource and subsidiary ratings in December 2024, primarily over Connecticut regulatory risk, though Moody's and Fitch moved outlooks to stable in mid-2026 after the Aquarion sale closed
Company plans $800M-$1.1B of incremental equity issuance through 2030 (plus ongoing DRIP/compensation issuance) to fund the capital plan, a modest drag on EPS growth
Large, growing debt load with material maturities; higher-for-longer rates increase interest expense (a cited driver of the Q3 2026 EPS miss) and raise the cost of funding the capital plan

regulatory.description: FERC's March 2026 Opinion No. 594 cut the New England transmission owners' base allowed ROE from 10.57% to 9.57% (incentive cap from 11.74% to 12.09%); Eversource is contesting the ruling, and the hit to 2026 EPS guidance was a primary driver of guidance cuts during the year, though a subsequent FERC order suspended a proposed increase pending further review

Separate, concurrent proceedings in CT (PURA), MA (DPU) and NH (PUC) create recurring event risk; CT in particular has pursued performance-based regulation reforms (post-Isaias) that give regulators broader authority over utility performance metrics and financial consequences
Disallowed and deferred storm costs, if later approved, are recovered via long-dated securitization (critics note multi-decade cost recovery), creating multi-year earnings and cash flow timing risk

macro.description: As a capital-intensive, dividend-paying utility, ES valuation and cost of capital are sensitive to the level and direction of long-term interest rates
Rising electric bills have become a political flashpoint in CT and MA, increasing pressure on regulators to constrain rate increases and storm cost recovery

The Trump administration's 2025 stop-work orders on offshore wind projects (Revolution Wind) demonstrated how federal permitting/policy reversals can still create financial exposure even after a company has divested ownership, via retained contractual obligations

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US regulated electric/gas utilities are in a multi-year capex supercycle driven by grid modernization, resiliency/storm-hardening, electrification and (in some regions) data center/large-load growth; New England specifically has modest native load growth but significant transmission investment needs tied to clean energy policy and aging infrastructure
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low - regulated utility earnings are largely non-cyclical and demand-inelastic, though storm costs, financing costs and regulatory cycles create idiosyncratic volatility
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - utility equity valuations trade inversely with long-term rates (bond-proxy characteristics), and financing costs for the large capital plan rise with rates
key_input_costs: Labor and contractor costs for T&D construction
Steel, copper, transformers and other grid equipment (tariff-exposed)
Natural gas commodity costs (passed through to gas distribution customers)

recent_developments.event: Reported Q3 2026 non-GAAP EPS of $0.92 (vs. ~$0.97 consensus, down from $0.99 a year earlier) on higher effective tax rate, higher interest expense, disallowed storm costs and a lower allowed transmission ROE; narrowed full-year 2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance to $4.62-$4.70 (midpoint $4.66) and reaffirmed 5-7% long-term EPS growth through 2030

PURA finalized a decision denying Eversource (CL&P) nearly $400 million in storm cost financing/carrying charges and disallowing roughly $500 million of its total storm cost recovery request; Eversource has appealed
Fitch revised Eversource's rating outlook from negative to stable

Moody's moved Eversource parent and NSTAR Electric outlooks from negative to stable, citing the completed Aquarion sale and approved Connecticut storm cost recovery progress; company booked a further ~$164 million charge tied to two 2025 federal stop-work orders on the Revolution Wind project

Completed the sale of Aquarion Water Company to the Aquarion Water Authority (a CT quasi-public authority) for a total purchase price of ~$2.4 billion (~$1.6B cash plus ~$800M net debt extinguished), generating ~$1.7 billion of net equity proceeds used to pay down debt; recorded an after-tax non-cash charge of ~$115 million ($0.31/share) in Q2 2026, smaller than the original ~$300 million 2024 estimate

FERC issued Opinion No. 594 cutting the New England transmission owners' allowed base ROE from 10.57% to 9.57% (incentive cap reduced from 11.74% to 12.09%), a material negative for Eversource's transmission segment economics; company is contesting the decision
Unveiled a $26.5 billion five-year (2026-2030) capital plan, up $2.3 billion from the prior $24.2 billion (2025-29) plan, concentrated in electric distribution and transmission

PURA issued a final decision in the Yankee Gas rate case, setting an allowed ROE of 9.32% (a 9.48% base reduced 16 bps for performance/management issues), well below the company's requested 10.3% plus a 50 bps risk premium

Trump administration issued two separate federal stop-work orders (August and December 2025) on the Revolution Wind project; a federal judge later ordered the August stop-work order lifted, but the episode drove incremental cost-sharing charges for Eversource despite its 2024 exit from project ownership

items.notes: Up from $4.57-$4.72 set after the Aquarion close in Q2 2026, which itself was cut from the original $4.80-$4.95 guided in February 2026, primarily reflecting the FERC transmission ROE reduction and loss of Aquarion earnings
Reaffirmed off the revised 2026 base; management expects to trend toward the upper half of the range by 2028

Up from $24.2B (2025-29) and $23.1B (2024-28); excludes Aquarion; concentrated in electric distribution (~$11B+) and transmission, plus incremental ~$700M of newly approved/ISO-NE-selected transmission projects as potential upside
Primary driver of the long-term EPS growth algorithm
Excludes ongoing DRIP/equity compensation issuance; funds the capital plan alongside debt and Aquarion sale proceeds

items.target: FFO-to-debt ~100 bps above S&P and Moody's downgrade thresholds
items.notes: Key credit-cushion target cited as supportive of the stable outlook revisions from Moody's and Fitch in mid-2026

guidance.management_commentary: Management has characterized the Aquarion sale and offshore wind exit as completing Eversource's transformation into a simplified, pure-play New England electric/gas T&D utility, directing proceeds to debt reduction. On the Q3 2026 call, management described the offshore wind cost-sharing overhang as largely resolved despite the 2025 stop-work order charges, pointed to CL&P rate case progress and Massachusetts AMI rollout (500,000+ meters installed) as supportive of the outlook, and reiterated confidence in reaching the upper half of the 5-7% long-term EPS growth range by 2028 even after absorbing the FERC transmission ROE cut.

bull_case: Simplified, de-risked pure-play regulated T&D utility after exiting water (Aquarion, June 2026) and offshore wind generation, with proceeds used to strengthen the balance sheet

Industry-leading ~$26.5 billion five-year capital plan (growing every year) supports an above-average ~8%+ rate base CAGR and a reaffirmed 5-7% long-term EPS growth target, with management guiding to the upper half of that range by 2028
Credit rating outlooks have turned stable (Moody's, Fitch) in 2026 after years of negative outlooks, reducing near-term downgrade risk

Performance-based rate mechanisms in Massachusetts and New Hampshire, plus a large FERC-regulated transmission base, offer more predictable earnings relative to the contentious Connecticut jurisdiction
Secular electrification tailwinds (EVs, heat pumps, grid modernization, potential large-load/data center interconnection) support continued above-trend capital investment demand across New England
bear_case: Connecticut remains a structurally adversarial regulatory jurisdiction - PURA has disallowed hundreds of millions in storm costs, cut allowed ROEs below requested levels, and drawn public criticism from the state's Attorney General, creating a persistent earned-vs-allowed ROE gap and litigation overhang
FERC's March 2026 cut to the New England transmission base ROE (10.57% to 9.57%) directly compressed transmission segment economics and has already forced multiple guidance cuts in 2026

Elevated leverage (debt/equity ~1.8x, net debt/EBITDA ~5.7x) combined with an expanding capital plan requires continued equity issuance and debt financing, a drag on EPS growth and a source of credit-rating sensitivity, particularly if rates stay elevated

Residual, hard-to-quantify offshore wind cost-sharing exposure on Revolution Wind (federal stop-work orders in 2025 already cost ~$164M-plus) shows that 'exited' legacy risks can still resurface and are sensitive to federal energy policy volatility

Consensus analyst sentiment is lukewarm (mostly Hold ratings, price targets clustered in the low-to-mid $70s) reflecting skepticism that the capital plan's growth can be delivered without further regulatory erosion or dilution
